paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Transposing a matrix flips it over its diagonal. The row number and the column number of every entry trade places, so rows become columns and columns become rows. The new matrix is called the transpose of A and is often written A^T. The British mathematician Arthur Cayley introduced the idea in 1858.

paragraphs.heading: Simple rules it follows
paragraphs.text: Flipping twice brings you back where you started, so the transpose undoes itself; an operation like this is called an involution. The transpose of a single number, or scalar, is just that same number. A square matrix and its transpose share the same determinant. If a matrix is invertible, its transpose is too, and the inverse of the transpose equals the transpose of the inverse.

paragraphs.heading: Multiplying a matrix by its flip
paragraphs.text: If A has m rows and n columns, multiplying it by its own transpose always gives a square matrix: A A^T is m × m, while A^T A is n × n. Both products are symmetric, meaning the entry in row i, column j equals the entry in row j, column i. Each entry of A A^T comes from pairing two rows of A. The entries in positions i, j and j, i come from the same two rows, so they are equal.

paragraphs.heading: A link to the dot product
paragraphs.text: The transpose ties matrices to the dot product. For two column vectors a and b, the dot product is the single entry of the matrix product a^T b. A related rule lets a matrix move across a dot product by turning into its transpose: (A a) ⋅ b = a ⋅ (A^T b).

paragraphs.heading: Transposing on a computer
paragraphs.text: On a computer, a program often never moves the numbers at all and simply reads the same data in a different order. Linear algebra libraries such as BLAS let you mark a matrix as one to be read in transposed order, which saves shuffling data around. Sometimes, though, physically rearranging the matrix in memory is worth it. When a matrix is stored row by row, each row sits together in memory but its columns are scattered. If an algorithm such as a fast Fourier transform works on the columns again and again, transposing the stored matrix first may make it run faster.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond grids of numbers
paragraphs.text: The main job of matrices is to stand for linear maps between finite-dimensional vector spaces, so the transpose can also be seen as an operation on those maps. That view leads to a broader definition that works for every linear map, including cases, such as infinite-dimensional spaces, where matrices cannot represent the map. In the finite-dimensional case the two pictures agree. The matrix of the transposed map is the transpose of the original map's matrix, whichever basis is chosen.
